newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Planned talks raise hopes for Indo-Pakistan thaw.
newsitem.headline: Planned talks raise hopes for Indo-Pakistan thaw.

text.p: The planned resumption of stalled peace talks between India and Pakistan later this month has raised hopes for a thaw in the frosty relations between the two arch-rivals.
But analysts cautioned on Friday against over-optimism.

Pakistan announced on Thursday that foreign ministry secretaries of the two governments would meet in New Delhi on March 28-31, and Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said he hoped to see a positive outcome from the exercise.

The last round of talks between the South Asian neighbours was in January 1994. They bogged down owing to differences over the disputed Himalayan region of Jammu and Kashmir, two-thirds of which is ruled by India and the rest by Pakistan.
The deadlock was broken after an exchange of conciliatory messages last month between Deve Gowda and new Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, whose nations have fought three wars.
"Good relations between Pakistan and India are essential for both the countries," a Pakistani analyst, Ataur Rehman, said on Friday.
"The economic conditions of India and Pakistan demand that they have better relations," he told Reuters.

But he said their dispute over Jammu and Kashmir -- the cause of two of the countries' three wars since they gained independence from Britain in 1947 -- was equally important and "until it is resolved, relations cannot improve".
"What makes the scenario more optimistic than it has been before is the atmosphere of expectation," commentator Khalid Mahmud wrote in the local daily News on Friday.

"Deve Gowda's United Front government, notwithstanding its dependence on the Congress (party) support for survival, is far more amenable to finding ways and means for improving relations with Pakistan and is certainly not overridden with New Delhi's customary big brother chauvinism in dealing with small neighbours," he said.
New Delhi, which is fighting a separatist Moslem revolt in its part of Kashmir, regards all of the region as an integral part of the Indian union.

But Islamabad, which denies New Delhi's charges of training and arming the rebels, wants the mainly Moslem Kashmiris to be allowed to vote in a U.N.-mandated plebiscite on whether to join Islamic Pakistan or Hindu-majority India.
No agenda has been announced for the March 28-31 meeting, though Sharif said in a message to Deve Gowda last month that it must prepare ground for an eventual meeting between them.

A terse Pakistani announcement simply said: "Pursuant to the exchange of letters between the prime ministers of Pakistan and India, it has been decided that the foreign secretaries of the two countries will meet in New Delhi on March 28-31."
Pakistan has insisted in the past that Kashmir was the "core issue" and must be on the agenda of any India-Pakistan dialogue.
India's insistence that its Kashmir claim is not negotiable is challenged with equal vehemence by Pakistan, which regards New Delhi as an aggressor in the state.
"We should not have normal relations with India until it vacates aggression in Kashmir," Agha Murtaza Pooya, a former chairman of Pakistan's state-funded Institute of Strategic Studies, told Reuters.
Pooya, also the editor-in-chief of Islamabad's The Muslim daily, opposed holding the Delhi talks without an ageda, and asked: "Why another meaningless round should be held."
But new Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub said on Tuesday that Kashmir would be on the agenda.
"Whatever the agenda...it will start and end at the Kashmir issue," he was quoted as telling local reporters. "The Kashmir issue is the sole cause for tension between the two countries."
The Press Trust of India news agency quoted Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral as saying in Mauritius on Friday that there were no preconditions for resuming the talks.
"There are no conditions on either side," he told Indian reporters accompanying him on the trip.
Gohar and Gujral are also due to meet in New Delhi on the sidelines of a two-day Non-Aligned Movement foreign ministers' conferences beginning there on April 7.
